title: The boy bound to the post
hookLine: a king promises a god his son, then stalls for years. Varuna, keeper of vows, comes to collect
carry: varuna keeps the vow, and loosens the bond

lines: NOT YET. NOT YET. NOT YET.
cards: A king with everything except a child makes a deal with a god: give me a son, and I'll give him back to you. The son is born. The god comes to collect.
And the king says, not yet, he's only a baby. Then, not yet, wait until his teeth come in. Then, wait until they fall out.
Anyone who has ever said we'll talk about it later knows the move. The god is Varuna. Today: the fourth voice, and a promise that comes due.

teach.b: The story is told in the Aitareya Brahmana, a prose text of the Rig Veda. King Harishchandra prays to Varuna, the god who keeps rita, the order of truth, and vows: if a son is born, I'll offer him to you.
Rohita is born, and the king stalls until the boy is grown. Then Rohita takes his bow and runs to the forest, and Varuna seizes the king with a swelling sickness.
Years later Rohita meets a starving sage, Ajigarta, and buys his middle son, Shunahshepa, for a hundred cows, to go in his place.
The boy is bound to the post. His own father comes forward with a knife. And Shunahshepa does the one thing left.

teach.h: EACH VERSE TO DAWN, A CORD FALLS.
teach.b: In the telling he goes from god to god, Prajapati, Agni, Savitr, Varuna, Indra, the Ashvins, and at last Ushas, the dawn, and with each verse to the dawn a cord falls away. With the last, he is free, and the king is well.
The sage Vishvamitra takes the boy as his own son.

teach.h: VRATA: A VOW IS A BOND.
teach.b: Hymns in the Rig Veda are credited to Shunahshepa, and one asks: loosen, Varuna, the upper bond, the middle, and the lowest. Here's the teaching.

In the hymns Varuna is dhritavrata, the one who holds to vows, and vrata is the word Hindus still use for a vow kept to God, a fast, a pilgrimage, a promise. A vow is a bond, and Varuna holds people to theirs.
But the same god who binds is the one who unties.

how: Many Hindus keep a vrata, a vow such as a weekly fast, a temple visit or a pilgrimage promised to God, and treat finishing it as serious; Rig Veda 1.24, credited to Shunahshepa, is part of Vedic recitation.

o: a king's tax law, carved on a pillar
a king's vow to Varuna, stalled until it came due
a love song from a prince to a dancer

games.q: the vow to Varuna — tap the pairs.
p: the king who vowed and stalled
the boy bound to the post
a vow, a promise kept to God

s: Harishchandra kept his vow to Varuna right away
he stalled again and again: when the baby's older, when his teeth come, when they fall out.
in the telling, Shunahshepa's bonds loosen as he prays to the dawn
with each verse to Ushas a cord fell away; with the last, he was free.
the word Hindus use for a vow or fast goes back to the hymns' vrata
Varuna is dhritavrata, holder of vows; a vrat today is a promise kept to God.

games.q: you made a vow to God when you were desperate. now things are fine and it's inconvenient. by Harishchandra's story, what fits?
o: keep it: a vow to God is a bond
games.why: Harishchandra's not yet ran for years and nearly cost a boy his life. Varuna holds people to their vows, and the story honors the one who turned and prayed.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you keep putting off: to a person, to God, or to yourself. Don't scold yourself. Just say it plainly, the way Harishchandra never did: this is what I said I'd do.
If you pray, borrow Shunahshepa's words: loosen what binds me, the upper, the middle, the lowest. If you don't, choose one small step toward keeping it today.

wordCard.voice: Hymns to Agni, and today, to Varuna: keeper of rita and of vows, who holds a stalling king to his word and unties a boy who prays. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a vow, an ordinance. In the hymns Varuna is dhritavrata, the one who holds to vows; today a vrat is a fast or vow kept to God.

carryVoice: Your line: varuna keeps the vow, and loosens the bond. A promise to God is worth keeping. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Aitareya Brahmana 7.13–18 (Harishchandra's vow to Varuna and his delays; Rohita flees; Varuna afflicts the king with dropsy; Shunahshepa bought for a hundred cows and bound; he praises god after god; his bonds loosen with the verses to Ushas; Vishvamitra adopts him)
Rig Veda 1.24.12–15 (Shunahshepa, seized and bound, called on Varuna; loosen the upper, middle and lowest bond)
Rig Veda 1.25.10 (Varuna dhritavrata, the one who holds to his vows)
